newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: World solar plans seen suffering lack of cash.
newsitem.headline: World solar plans seen suffering lack of cash.

text.p: Ambitious plans unveiled at a world solar summit aiming to provide electricity for all by the middle of the next century are likely to develop slowly due to lack of cash, analysts and delegates said on Wednesday.

They said pledges of political support given at the two-day meeting, which ended in Zimbabwe on Tuesday, were not enough to attract crucial investment into solar and other renewable sources of energy as initially hoped by some conference organisers.

"The whole programme, like many other programmes, will depend on financial support and I don't think anybody has illusions that this will be found in abundance," Zimbabwean economic consultant John Robertson said.
"It (solar programme) will develop slowly because, I think, many investors are not persuaded this is a fast-growing sector," he told Reuters.

Host Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe closed the historic conference, appealing to Western donors, rich countries, Third World governments and private industry to help fund global plans to provide solar, wind, geothermal and other sources of renewable energy to 2.4 billion people living without electricity worldwide.

Mugabe said without funding, the plans were worthless proposals, supporting several delegates who had shifted the focus to the financial mechanism to develop energy sources which the conference advocated as generally cheaper, environmentally friendly and more accessible than most.

In a statement to the Harare conference, the World Bank, which recently pledged its support for such plans, said their success would depend largely on development of local financing mechanisms and formulation of appropriate policies.
"Experience shows that the need is for small amounts of financing, delivered with precision at the retail level, or in somewhat larger amounts to capitalise dealers," it said.

International Energy Agency executive director Robert Priddle said the Third World's answer to financial problems lay in opening itself to foreign investment to develop the required solar and other renewable energy sources.

"Major private sector investment will be essential (and) those with the vision to liberalise energy markets and open up to outside investment would create exciting opportunities," he said, also backing calls to mobilise domestic savings through sound economic management for this purpose.
Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa said progress would be slow because many Third World nations were cash-strapped.

The World Solar Summit -- attended by over 100 delegates, including 12 heads of state and governments and jointly organised by Zimbabwe and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) -- was initially called to drum up political support for solar use.

The delegates pledged strong political support and urged the conference onto the difficult path of finding finance for about 300 projects presented under a 1996-2005 UNESCO World Solar Programme, and other long-term projects.

According to the United Nations, about 18 percent of the globe's primary energy currently comes from renewable sources, but UNESCO says greater use could push this figure to between 25 and 35 percent by the year 2050.
